What goes wrong when the Sales department moves to another floor, when you want to record a new department that has no employees yet, and when the last employee of a department leaves? turns.prompt: A least-recently-used (LRU) cache with a fixed capacity is often built from a hash map plus a doubly linked list of entries ordered by last use. What does each part contribute? Walk through what happens on a cache hit for key k, and explain why both get and put can run in O(1) time on average.
turns.answer: The hash map gives O(1) average lookup from a key to its node, while the doubly‑linked list maintains the recency ordering so the most‑recent entry is at the head and the least‑recent at the tail; on a hit the map yields the node, which is unlinked from its current position and re‑inserted at the head in a constant number of pointer updates, and on a put we either update‑move an existing node the same way or insert a new node at the head (removing the tail node and its map entry if we exceed capacity), so both get and put consist only of a few hash‑map and pointer operations and therefore run in O(1) average time.

grade.rationale: The candidate correctly explained the roles of both the hash map and the doubly linked list, detailed the constant-time pointer updates required on a hit, and explained why both operations run in O(1) time on average.

provisional_grade.rationale: The candidate correctly explained the roles of both the hash map and the doubly linked list, detailed the constant-time pointer updates required on a hit, and explained why both operations run in O(1) time on average.
